nameStory: The Bloody Sap Beetle earned its dramatic name from the reddish or orange spots that mark its dark body, creating a blood-spatter effect against its black background. Like other sap beetles, it feeds on tree sap, fermenting fruit, and other sweet, sticky substances that would make your fingers tacky to the touch.
description: The Bloody Sap Beetle is a small, oval-shaped beetle about the size of a ladybug, typically measuring around 3-6 millimeters long. Its shiny black body is decorated with distinctive reddish-orange spots that give it its memorable name. Like other sap beetles, it has a somewhat flattened appearance and short, clubbed antennae that end in wider segments. You'll often find these little beetles crawling around on tree wounds, overripe fruit, or fermenting plant matter where they feed on sugary liquids.

idTips.label: Distinctive spots
idTips.description: Look for bright reddish-orange or yellowish spots on a shiny black background - the contrast is quite striking and the spots often appear almost translucent when light hits them

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small oval beetle about the size of a peppercorn, with a slightly flattened body that feels smooth and hard if you gently touch it

idTips.label: Clubbed antennae
idTips.description: Short antennae that get wider at the tips, forming distinct clubs - you can see this clearly if the beetle is still or moving slowly

idTips.label: Shiny surface
idTips.description: The body has a glossy, almost metallic sheen that reflects light, making the beetle appear polished

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often found crawling on sticky, sweet-smelling tree sap, rotting fruit, or fungal growths where you can smell fermentation

habitat: Look for Bloody Sap Beetles in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, especially around wounded or diseased trees where sap is flowing. They're commonly found on oak, maple, and birch trees, as well as in areas with fallen, fermenting fruit like old apple orchards or wild cherry groves. You might also spot them on bracket fungi growing on dead wood, particularly in moist woodland areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging to feed on fresh tree sap from winter-damaged bark and early fermenting plant matter.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen feeding on tree wounds, overripe berries, and fungal growths. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early autumn, often found on fermenting fallen fruit and late-season tree sap flows before seeking winter shelter.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter under bark, in leaf litter, or other protected spots and are rarely seen during cold months.

funFact: Bloody Sap Beetles are essentially nature's tiny bartenders - they're attracted to fermenting tree sap and fruit that contains alcohol, and they can actually tolerate alcohol levels that would be harmful to many other insects!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with its close relatives, the Picnic Beetle and Four-spotted Sap Beetle, but the Bloody Sap Beetle's spots tend to be more orange-red rather than yellow, and they're often less clearly defined than the neat four spots of the Four-spotted Sap Beetle. Memory trick: 'Bloody' beetles have reddish spots, not yellow ones.
compareHints: Unlike its cousin the Picnic Beetle which has yellow spots arranged in bands across its body, the Bloody Sap Beetle has more orange-red spots that can be irregularly placed. The Four-spotted Sap Beetle lives up to its name with exactly four distinct yellow spots, while the Bloody Sap Beetle may have varying numbers of reddish spots that sometimes merge together. The Bloody Sap Beetle also tends to be found more often on tree sap rather than at picnics or on exposed fruit.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Picnic beetles can be distinguished from their close relatives by their specific banding pattern - the bloody sap beetle tends to have reddish markings rather than yellow bands, while the four-spotted sap beetle has distinct spots rather than bands.
The Four-spotted Sap Beetle is easily distinguished from its close relative, the Picnic Beetle, by those four distinctive spots - Picnic Beetles have zigzag yellow bands instead.
